Section (1) Oxygen Therapy
1.1 Introduction to Oxygen Therapy

rows: Hypoxaemia means low levels of oxygen in the blood (low blood oxygen saturation or
content).
Hypoxia is inadequate oxygen in tissues for normal cell and organ function, and hypoxia
results from hypoxaemia.
hypoxaemia is a life-threatening condition that requires early detection and treatment, As all
the functions of the human body require oxygen, oxygen deprivation can have severe adverse
effects on the cells that perform important biological processes. Lack of oxygen leads very
quickly to dysfunction of the organ systems, and death.
partial oxygen pressure (PaO2) is a measure only of oxygen molecules dissolved in plasma
and not of those bound to haemoglobin. however, as there is a dynamic equilibrium between
freely dissolved and haemoglobin-bound oxygen molecules, oxygen saturation can be
calculated from the PaO2
Arterial oxygen saturation is referred to as SaO2 when measured by gas analysis and as
SpO2 when measured by pulse oximetry.
The normal range of SpO2 at sea level is 97–99%, with a lower limit (mean minus 2 standard
deviations) of 94%.
The “gold standard” for measuring arterial oxygen tension (PaO2) and for calculating
oxygen saturation is blood gas analysis.
When to Give Oxygen?
In practice, the threshold at which oxygen is given is often SpO2 < 90%, which corresponds
to the flat part of the haemoglobin–oxygen dissociation curve, and represents a safe margin of
error where there are sufficient oxygen supplies. Small reductions in SpO2 below 90% may
represent a dangerous fall in PaO2 (steep part of the curve).

t: 1.2 Detection of Hypoxemia
clinical signs
• central cyanosis
• nasal flaring
• grunting with every breath
• depressed mental state (i.e. drowsy, lethargic).
• less specific signs for hypoxaemia:
o fast breathing (respiratory rate of 70/min or more)
o severe lower chest wall indrawing
o head nodding
Pulse oximetry is the most accurate non-invasive method for detecting hypoxaemia. It is used
to measure the percentage of oxygenated haemoglobin in arterial blood (SpO2 )
Blood gas analysis is another very accurate method for detecting hypoxaemia. It is used to
measure the partial pressure of oxygen (PaO2 )
1.3 Equipment for Giving Oxygen

rows: Nasal prongs

• Standard flow rates through nasal prongs are 0.5–1 L/min for neonates,
• Humidification is not required with standard oxygen flow rates, as the natural nasal
mechanisms heat and humidify the inspired oxygen
• There is a slight risk that the airway will become obstructed by mucus (35), especially
if a high flow with no humidification is used.
• The fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2 ) 2 depends on the oxygen flow rate, the
relation between prong and nasal diameters and the patient’s body weight,
• In infants weighing up to 10 kg, oxygen flows of 0.5 L/min, 1 L/min and 2 L/min
result in FiO2 values of about 35% 45% and 55%, respectivel
• Achievement of PEEP depends on the distal prong diameter, the oxygen flow and
body weight. Whereas 1 L/min of oxygen may produce a PEEP of about 5 cm H2 O
in premature infants, there is no significant PEEP production with the same flow in
infants weighing up to 10 kg

• The distal prong should fit well into the nostril (premature infants: 1 mm, infants
weighing up to 10 kg: 2 mm). The prongs should be secured with a piece of tape on
the cheeks near the nose
A nasal catheter

• is a thin, flexible tube that is passed into the nose and ends with its tip in the nasal
cavity
• The oxygen does not have to be humidified because the tip of the catheter lies in the
nasal cavity. Catheters can become blocked with mucus, which can cause upper
airway obstruction.
• There is little risk of displacement into the oesophagus, with a consequent risk of
gastric distension. Ideally, a nasogastric tube should be in place to decompress the
stomach if distension occurs
• In neonates and infants, 8-French (F) size catheters should be used
• A catheter passed for a distance equal to the distance from the side of the nostril to the
inner margin of the eyebrow usually reaches the posterior part of the nasal cavity.
• The tip of the catheter should not be visible below the uvula.
Nasopharyngeal catheters

• passed to the pharynx just below the level of the uvula, better oxygenation is achieved
with a lower oxygen flow than with nasal prongs
• Nasopharyngeal catheters are inserted into the nose to a depth 1 cm less than the
distance from the side of the nose to the front of the ear (tragus)
• because of the relatively high FiO2 in the trachea and significant PEEP production: in
infants, 1 L/min of nasopharyngeal oxygen given through an 8-F catheter produces a
PEEP of 2.8 cm H2 O
• in most settings where frequent monitoring is difficult, nasal prongs or nasal catheters
are the preferred method
• Nasopharyngeal catheters are prone to blockage with mucus, and accumulation of
mucus can cause upper airway obstruction
• As oxygen given through a nasopharyngeal catheter bypasses the humidifying and
warming properties of the nose, effective external humidification is essential to avoid
drying of the pharyngeal mucosa and to reduce the likelihood of thickened secretions
blocking the catheter
• Nasopharyngeal catheters can be displaced downwards into the oesophagus and cause
gagging, vomiting and gastric distension. Their use should therefore be limited to
situations in which nasal prongs are unavailable
Oxygen Blender System

• System that delivers low flow oxygen therapy
• Administration of a controlled and continuous flow of oxygen
• Flow is less than the patient’s peak inspiratory flow
• Usually administered using a nasal cannula
• Indicated for mild hypoxemia with mild respiratory distress
• Allows you to optimize tissue oxygenation while minimizing oxygen toxicity
• Achieved by the Vayu blender
• Allows titration of oxygen concentration
• Treatment with low-flow oxygen therapy is monitored using pulse oximetry. The goal
is to achieve and maintain an oxygen saturation of above 88% while using the lowest
oxygen concentration possible.
• Breathing pure oxygen can harm the lungs, leading to bronchopulmonary dysplasia.
It can also harm the eyes, causing retinopathy of prematurity, and in severe cases, it
can even lead to brain damage.

t: 2.1 Introduction for NIV

rows: Moving from an era of invasive ventilation to that of non-invasive respiratory support,
various modalities have emerged resulting in improved neonatal outcome.
Over the past few decades, invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) has been replaced by non-
invasive ventilation (NIV) as IMV has been shown to be associated with major morbidities
e.g.: bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) which is adversely related to pulmonary
hypertension, increased susceptibility to respiratory infection, neurodevelopmental
impairment and cerebral palsy.
Definition and concept of NIV
Non-invasive respiratory ventilation is the standard respiratory support for preterm and term
infants. The type of NIV used is based on the severity of respiratory distress, risk of treatment
failure, gestational age, and timing of application. HFNC, CPAP, NIPPV (synchronized or
non-synchronized) are the most used NIV in the newborn. BiPAP, Nasal HFOV and NAVA
are infrequently used and need further evaluation before routine application. Early initiation,
adequate and aggressive use of surfactant/caffeine, optimum warm idification, appropriate
nasal interface, and nursing care are crucial in the success of NIV.
NIV refers to any method of providing respiratory support, where an endotracheal tube is not
used. The various methods include oxygen administration through a hood box or nasal
cannula, heated, humidified high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC or HFNC), nasal CPAP
(nCPAP), nasal intermittent positive-pressure ventilation (NIPPV), nasal bilevel positive
airway pressure (nBiPAP), nasal high-frequency oscillatory ventilation (nHFOV), and nasal
neurally adjusted ventilator assist (nNAVA). All these devices are driven by a gas flow,
which can be with or without a pressure generator (HFNC); pressure generated at a single
level (CPAP) or at two levels (NIPPV and BiPAP).
Modalities of NIV are commonly used in neonates

t: Advantages of NIV:

rows: 1- Preservation of airway integrity: (NIV flow stents the airway and prevents collapse) NIV
avoids the need for invasive ventilation and reduces the risk of complications associated
with it.
2- Reduced risk of ventilator-associated complications: such as ventilator-associated
pneumonia and lung injury.( by avoiding endotracheal intubation and retention of tracheal
secretion )
3- Enhanced parental involvement: NIV allowing neonates to be accessible and fostering
bonding. ( such as kangaroo care )
4- Improved respiratory muscle’s function: NIV supports the neonate’s respiratory effort and
potentially preserves respiratory muscle function. ( by minimising work of breathing)
5- Enhance gas exchange: NIV specially CPAP, can improve oxygenation and carbon
dioxide elimination by ( creating and maintaining a PEEP, ) maintaining open airways
and promoting alveolar recruitment.
6- Decreased risk of chronic lung disease: use of NIV may reduce the risk of chronic lung in
premature infants by minimising lung injury associated with invasive ventilation.
7- Better tolerance in preterm infants.
8- Decreased need for intubation: NIV can help to avoid or reduce the duration of invasive
ventilation and its associated complications.
( can be put or mentioned before adv. 2. )
9- Flexibility in management: NIV provides flexibility in adjusting respiratory support
according to the neonate’s respiratory needs.
10- Potential for earlier weaning: NIV facilitates the transition to spontaneous breathing and
reduces the duration of ventilatory support.

t: Disadvantages of NIV

rows: 1- Mask interface challenges: neonate may experience difficulty tolerating the mask
interface , leading to leak or skin breakdown ( interface care and prevention of trauma )
2- Gastric distention can result in regurgitation and aspiration.
3- Nasal injury: use of nasal prongs can cause nasal trauma, irritation or septal necrosis,
particularly with prolonged use.
4- Discomfort and agitation.
5- Difficulty in synchrony. ( No flow sensor as in IMV)
6- Limited ventilatory support. ( NIV failure can occur
7- Risk of air leak. ( the pressure that reach the lungs cannot be measured, some babies may
have auto-PEEP that increase the risk of air leaks)
8- Need for skilled monitoring. ( Bed side nurses should be trained for NIV care and
monitoring )

t: Indication of NIV in neonates

rows: 1- Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS): NIV is often used to support premature infants
with RDS, providing respiratory assistance and maintaining adequate oxygenation.
2- Transient Tachypnoea of Newborn (TTN): NIV can be employed to assist neonates
with TTN, a condition characterised by rapid breathing due to delayed clearance of
lung fluid.
3- Meconium Aspiration Syndrome (MAS): neonates with MAS may require NIV to
support breathing and improve oxygenation.
4- Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn (PPHN): NIV may be used in the
management of PPHN to enhance oxygenation and reduce pulmonary vascular
resistance.
5- Bronchiolitis: infants with bronchiolitis, often caused by Respiratory Syncytial Virus
(RSV), may benefit from NIV to alleviate respiratory distress.
6- Apnoea of Prematurity: Continuous Positive Airway Pressure CPAP is commonly
used to manage apnoea of prematurity and maintain respiratory stability in preterm
infants.
7- Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia (CDH): NIV can be part of respiratory support
strategy for neonates with CDH, helping to manage respiratory distress associated
with this anomaly.
8- Post-operative support: following certain surgical procedures, neonates may require
NIV to assist with respiratory support during the recovery period.
9- Neuromuscular disorders: infant with neuromuscular conditions affecting respiratory
muscles may benefit from NIV to support breathing.
10- It’s important to tailor the choice of NIV methods and settings based on the clinical
needs of the neonates. Regular monitoring and adjustments are crucial to ensure
effective respiratory support and over all well-being.

t: Contraindication of NIV:

rows: 1- Severe respiratory distress: if a neonate is in severe respiratory distress, especially
when accompanied by cardiovascular instability, NIV may not be appropriate, and
invasive ventilation might be required.

2- Haemodynamic instability: neonates with unstable cardiovascular status or severe
haemodynamic compromise may be contraindicated for NIV, as positive pressure
ventilation can affect cardiac function.
3- Severe air leak syndrome: neonates with significant air leaks, such as pneumothorax
or pneumomediastinum, may require invasive ventilation, as positive pressure from
NIV could worsen these conditions.
4- Facial abnormalities or anomalies: facial anomalies that prevent proper mask seal or
interface placement may hinder the effectiveness of NIV.
5- Unstable neurological status: in neonates with unstable neurological conditions,
cautious evaluation is necessary, as NIV may not be suitable for those unable to
tolerate the treatment.
6- Upper airway obstruction: conditions causing significant airway obstruction may
limit the effectiveness of the NIV or pose risks, and alternative strategies may need
consideration.
7- Gastrointestinal conditions: neonates with abdominal wall anomalies or massive
abdominal distention may experience increased risk of complications with NIV.
8- Inability to protect airway: if a neonate cannot protect their airway, NIV may not be
suitable, and consideration for invasive ventilation might be necessary.
9- Uncooperative neonate: NIV requires the neonate’s cooperation and tolerance, and in
cases of extreme agitation or non-compliance, alternative strategies may be needed.
Always consult with neonatal specialist/ senior and consider the individual patient’s clinical
status, as contraindications can vary based on specific circumstances. Regular assessment and
monitoring are essential when employing NIV in neonatal care.

2.2 High-Flow Nasal Cannula (HFNC)
HFNC works by providing inhaled gases at flows higher than the inspiratory demand flow.
This leads to wash out of upper airways, reduces physiological dead space, and decreases
nasopharyngeal airway resistance. It also provides variable positive end expiratory pressure
and decreases work of breathing. But, as delivering HFNC requires a loose-fitting nasal
prong, the pressure delivery is not reliable. The three important components of HFNC include
✔ a flow generator,
✔ an air-oxygen blender, and
✔ a heater-humidifier.
HFNC has gained popularity because of the ease of use, lesser nasal trauma, and more
comfort to the neonate.

rows: HFNC can be used effectively for different purposes (different modalities):

t: ● as primary respiratory support (immediately after birth)
● Post extubation from IMV: weaning modality)
● as a weaning modality from other types of NIV
● During endotracheal intubation
HFNC for primary respiratory support
HFNC has been compared with CPAP as a primary respiratory support modality for
preterm infants diagnosed with respiratory distress soon after birth. The Cochrane review
reported on the outcomes of risk of mortality or BPD, mortality, BPD, treatment failure
within the first 72 h and the need for IMV. The authors found that the use of HFNC as a
primary respiratory support did not result in any significant difference in most of the
outcomes except for a higher treatment failure rate in the HFNC group when compared to the
CPAP group. Also, HFNC was associated with a decreased risk of nasal injury when
compared to CPAP. In conclusion, the use of HFNC as primary support in infants with ≥28
weeks GA may not result in any difference in the combined outcome of mortality or BPD
when compared to CPAP. However, HFNC might be associated with an increased risk of
need for upgradation of respiratory support within 72 h of initiation. There is no robust
evidence for the use of HFNC as primary respiratory support in extreme low gestational age
newborns.
HFNC for post extubation support
HFNC has also been used as a weaning modality after extubation from IMV and its efficacy
has been compared with other modes of NIV. The recently published meta-analysis by
Martins et al. (7 studies, 1,044 infants) compared HFNC vs. CPAP. The primary outcomes
were extubation failure rates at 72 h and 7 days. They reported no significant difference in the
primary outcomes. The other outcomes of mortality, BPD, air leak syndrome, pneumothorax
and abdominal distension were also similar between the groups. As observed in the other
systematic reviews on primary respiratory support, HFNC was associated with a decreased
risk of nasal injury. Likewise for primary respiratory support, the use of HFNC as a post-
extubation modality requires further trials in the sub-group of ELGANs.
HFNC as a weaning mode from other NIV modalities

rows: There is no consensus on the timing or method of weaning from various NIV respiratory
support modalities. Various methods like abrupt stoppage of CPAP, gradual lowering of
PEEP, intermediate stoppage of CPAP for some time followed by re-application, weaning to
HFNC, weaning to low flow nasal cannula or head box oxygen have been tried. But none of
the strategies have been conclusively shown to be better.

t: HFNC during endotracheal intubation
Intubation of a hypoxemic neonate is often associated with adverse life-threatening events.
The use of HFNC during endotracheal intubation has been compared to standard care (no
nasal high flow or use of supplemental oxygen) in a recently published RCTs
Improved success rate: The use of HFNC during the procedure improved the
likelihood of a successful first-attempt intubation.
Reduced physiological instability: Neonates in the HFNC group were more likely to
remain stable during the procedure compared to those receiving standard care.
2.3 Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP)

rows: Definition is a non-invasive method for applying a constant distending pressure level (above
atmospheric) during inhalation and exhalation to support spontaneously breathing newborn
infants.
Introduction
The earliest documented use of CPAP in preterm neonates for providing respiratory support
was in 1971 by Gregory et al. Subsequently, with the introduction and refinement of IMV in
neonates, use of CPAP declined in the subsequent decade. This trend changed with the
landmark publication by Avery et al. in 1987 (11). They reported the incidence of chronic
lung disease (BPD) in 8 tertiary care neonatal intensive care units (NICUs) in North America,
specifically to evaluate the likely causes for the difference in the incidence of BPD between
these NICUs. The group found that the University of Columbia which used CPAP quite
extensively with restricted IMV use had the lowest incidence of BPD. This reinvigorated the
interest in CPAP globally, with its use being researched in various disease settings in
neonates.

t: The mechanism of action of CPAP:

rows: • It improves the functional residual capacity (FRC) and hence decreases the work of
breathing.
• It decreases intrapulmonary shunting.
• It stabilizes the compliant chest wall of preterm neonates and splints the airway.
• It decreases thoraco-abdominal asynchrony in the neonate.
• It aids in accelerating the growth of the immature lung and improves protein content per
gram of the lung tissue.
• It reduces alveolar Edema, conserves surfactant and decreases the occurrence of apnoea,
especially in preterm infants.

• Nasal CPAP is usually started at a pressure of 5 cm H O, flow of 5 L/min and fraction of
2

inhaled oxygen (FiO ) of 30%. Following this, the CPAP is titrated to reduce the work of
2
breathing, flow to obtain adequate bubbling (continuous bubbling in both phases of

respiration) and FiO to achieve the saturation targets (90%–95% for preterm neonates).

t: Components of CPAP:

rows: (a) flow generator: A source of warm, humidified, blended air-oxygen mixture with an
inline flow generator is present. The flow could be either constant or variable.
(b) positive pressure generator device: The positive pressure delivered during CPAP may
be generated through one of the following techniques:
• The expiratory valve of the ventilator which adjusts the expiratory pressure.
• Adjustment of the inspiratory flow through flow drivers or ventilators.
• The Bubble CPAP system produces a positive pressure by placing the far end of the
expiratory tubing under water. The pressure is adjusted by altering the depth of the tube under
the surface of the water.
(b) a Humidifier To maintain temperature between 36.8 to 37.4
(d) airway interface: Following nasal interfaces are used in neonates:
• Long nasal prongs/nasopharyngeal prongs.
• Short binasal prongs.
• Nasal masks.

t: Types of CPAP:

rows:
•
Bubble CPAP: In B-CPAP the positive pressure in the circuit is achieved by simply
submerging the distal expiratory tubing into a known depth of water column.
•
Ventilator CPAP: In V-CPAP where an expiratory valve on the ventilator is adjusted
to provide resistance to the flow of air.
•
variable flow ventilator CPCP: Baseline flow & expiratory valve of the ventilator
regulate minimal pressure fluctuation.
•
Infant flow driver: By applying high flow gas under pressure via a large pore nasal
device into the infant’s nostrils (It reduces work of breathing).

t: Indication of CPAP :
▪ CPAP application in the Delivery room (DR) Earlier, extremely preterm and very
preterm neonates were routinely intubated, and given surfactant in the Delivery Room
prophylactically. The current evidence suggests that early use of CPAP in the DR with
selective use of early rescue surfactant using lesser invasive modalities is beneficial and
preferable over prophylactic surfactant use followed by IMV in preterm neonates.
• Use of DR CPAP compared to IMV with or without surfactant has decreased the
risk of the combined outcome of BPD or death, BPD alone and failure of
treatment with no effect on the outcomes of mortality, pulmonary air leak or IVH
grade >2.
▪ CPAP for RDS as primary respiratory support
• CPAP for management of neonates with RDS should be initiated in the Delivery
Room and continued while the neonate is being shifted to the NICU.
▪ CPAP for apnea of prematurity
• CPAP reduce the incidence of mixed and obstructive apnea in preterm neonates. It
has also reduce the frequency and duration of desaturation episodes in central
apnea
▪ CPAP for transient tachypnea of newborn (TTN)
• CPAP helps in TTN by facilitating the clearance of lung fluid and helps to reduce
the duration of NICU stay.
▪ CPAP for meconium aspiration syndrome (MAS)
• CPAP helps in maintaining FRC and prevent atelectasis in MAS.

● Continuous heart rate, respiratory rate and oxygen saturation monitoring should be in

rows: ● An oro-gastric tube should be used in preference to a naso-gastric tube, to prevent

aspirated prior to feed to empty gas and reduce the risk of abdominal distension,
although CPAP rarely causes a distended abdomen
● If a baby is not being fed, the oro-gastric tube should be aspirated a minimum of every

syringe barrel on the end, but you may get stomach contents passed up through it..

● Ensure that the face is kept clean and free from secretions
● Ensure the area behind a baby’s ears is kept clean, as very preterm babies may be
nursed with a CPAP hat on 24 hours a day for many weeks in a row
● If transferring a baby on CPAP within a hospital or between hospitals refer to local
transportation guidelines and policies
● If there is a significant change in a baby’s support requirement or respiratory status,
inform the medical staff and the nurse in charge, as this may be indicative of a more
serious problem
● CPAP can be an uncomfortable and unpleasant experience for babies due to the loud
noise levels, high gas flow through the mouth and nose, restricted head movements
and obstructed faces. Staff should be vigilant for signs of pain and discomfort or
distress and should seek to modify baby’s environment and offer developmental care
where appropriate. For example, kangaroo care, nesting, non-nutritive sucking,
containment holding or a cuddle.

t: 2.4 Monitoring for Infants Nursed on CPAP

rows: Every hour check visually:

● The nose should not be squashed or pushed upwards
● The eyes should be clearly visible
● Tapes should not be too tight and should certainly not cause indentation, pitting or
ocular oedema
At least four hourly checks physically:

● The hat should be checked for tightness and correct fit regularly – it should not be too
tight or too loose or rub against the infant’s skin
● Prongs/Mask should be removed from the nose to allow rest from the pressure on it,
more often if the infant’s condition dictates
● The nose should be inspected for signs of redness, skin breakdown, bruising,
indentation, altered shape and bleeding. Any alteration in appearance should be
documented
● Prongs/Mask should be checked to ensure that they are clean and patent, prior to
being replaced on the infant
● The ears should be inspected to ensure that they are not creased or folded. They
should also be inspected for signs of skin breakdown, redness, bruising, swelling,
discharge or bleeding. Any alteration in appearance should be documented
IMPORTANT Remember:

● Prongs/Mask should be removed by loosening of the tapes rather than pulling
them straight off the infant’s face
● Regular mouth care should be performed
● Suctioning should NOT be routine but as dictated by the infant
● It is important that documentation is completed when the nose is checked and
any changes noted

t: 2.5 Assess and manage for nasal injury
There should be careful monitoring of skin integrity of the nares, as there is a definite risk of
damage to the external skin and/or internal membranes of the nose.
Best practice for nose care is for the nose and surrounding area to be assessed and scored on
an hourly basis, so that evidence of skin breakdown is identified quickly and managed
appropriately.
The score should be documented in a predetermined place, the ITU/HDU observation chart
would be an appropriate place
If there are changes to the nose or surrounding area:

rows: 1. Check that all of the above have been followed – that the hat/mask/prongs are the
correct size and are clean and patent. That there is no error with the set-up of the
CPAP. Document and recheck in 1-2 hours depending on severity.
2. Recheck – have there been any changes? Has it improved or deteriorated? If
improved, document and continue to recheck regularly, minimum of every four
hours. If deteriorated, inform the nurse in charge and medical staff, document.
3. Try increasing time off to relieve pressure, consider facial oxygen if needed. Consider
using Vapotherm if available or alternating masks and prongs. Consider a dressing or
treatment to the affected area. Document any changes in care.
4. Consider elective intubation and ett CPAP /ventilation. Inform tissue viability nurses
and plastic surgeons. Complete an incident form. Document any changes in care.

t: 2.6 Nasal (synchronized) intermittent positive pressure
ventilation (NIPPV)

rows: Nasal (synchronized) intermittent positive pressure ventilation (s)NIPPV is defined as any
mode of assisted ventilation that delivers pressure throughout the respiratory cycle without
endotracheal intubation; with or without synchronization of neonatal breathing.
In NIPPV, the pressure is delivered at two levels [peak inspiratory pressure (PIP) and PEEP]
using a mechanical ventilator, by modulating the gas flow and orifice of the expiratory valve.
NIPPV therefore augments nCPAP with superimposed inflations to a set PIP [55]. High
nCPAP failure rates have prompted neonatologists to seek other more effective NIV
modalities.

Section (3) Mechanical Ventilation
3.1 INTRODUCTION to MV:
⮚ Knowledge and skills of invasive ventilation in NICU are essential requirements for
medical staff working in intensive care unit.
⮚ This section is intended to provide the trainees with essentials and basics of the art of
neonatal mechanical ventilation, aiming for safe practice.
⮚ The responsibility of the intensivist is to optimize ventilation and prevent harmful
effect of over or under-ventilation.
Objectives of MV Section:
1. To know the basic physiology of respiration.
2. To be familiar with some of the common ventilation terminology.
3. To understand the concept and common principals of mechanical ventilation.
4. To be aware of common types and modes of mechanical ventilation.
5. To know the common indications of mechanical ventilation.
6. To develop skills needed to use the mechanical ventilator safely from initiation to
weaning and extubation.
7. To know how to improve the care of the ventilated babies and to monitor them.
8. To be familiar with the common complications of the mechanical ventilator and how
to prevent them.
3.2 Physiology and lung mechanics:
Normal Breathing and Lung Mechanics The main function of the respiratory system is to
remove CO2 from and add O2 to systemic venous blood brought to the lung. For air to flow
into and out of the lungs a pressure gradient is always required ( delta P )
In normal spontaneous respiration, air is drawn from the atmosphere into the alveoli because
of negative intra-pleural pressure generated by contraction of the diaphragm and intercostal
muscles during inspiration and released from alveoli into the atmosphere during expiration by
pressure generated from elastic recoil of the lung.
What is a normal breath? A breath is defined as one cycle of flow of gas into the lung
(inspiration) and flow of gas out of the lungs ( exhalation ).
Phases of breathing: A breath has 4 phases:
1. Initiation of breath:
Initiation of a breath is called triggering and the factor or variable that initiated the breath is
the trigger.
A normal spontaneous breath is triggered by neurological and chemical triggers and is
usually spontaneous.
2. Inspiratory Phase:
• During inspiratory phase the air continues to flow and the lung volume increases until
the pressure reaches a peak and sustains for some time then the flow stops and
inspiration is terminated.
• The period from the start of the inspiration to the termination of inspiration (start of
exhalation) is the inspiratory time (Ti),
3. CYCLING
• The switch from the end of inspiration to the start of exhalation is called cycling,
• For a spontaneous breath, both trigger and cycling are controlled by neural output
from the respiratory centers in the brainstem, modified by inputs from
mechanoreceptors and chemoreceptors.
4. Expiatory phase
• Exhalation during normal spontaneous breath is passive resulting from alveolar
pressure generated by elastic recoil of the lung and chest wall.
• The time from the start of exhalation to start of new cycle is the expiratory time (Ti),
Respiratory Mechanics:
⮚ Respiratory mechanics refer to the expression of lung function through measures of
pressure and flow. From these, a variety of derived indices can be determined, such as
flow, pressure, volume, compliance, resistance, and work of breathing (WOB). These
factors directly affect lung volumes and therefore functional residual capacity (FRC)
and gas exchange.
⮚ Mechanical properties of the respiratory system govern the principles of air
movement between the alveoli and the atmosphere.
⮚ Along with pressure, knowledge of lung volumes and capacities is crucial to
understand normal lung function as well as many pathological conditions.
⮚ Tidal volume (VT): is the volume of gas moved with each breath. In healthy neonate,
spontaneous VT is usually between 4-6 ml/kg. This volume refreshes alveolar gas
with atmospheric air during inspiration and leads to removal of CO2 during
exhalation; (VENTILATION).
⮚ The volume of gas remaining in the lung after tidal exhalation is termed functional
residual capacity (FRC). It acts as a reservoir for gas exchange between the alveoli
and the pulmonary capillary blood throughout respiration. Decreasing lung
compliance will lower FRC and leads to profound effects on OXYGENATION.
⮚ Residual volume (RV): is the volume of gas remaining in the lung after a maximal
forced exhalation.
⮚ Positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP): is the positive pressure that will remain
in the airways at the end of exhalation. It helps maintain end-expiratory volume and
⮚ Peak Inspiratory Pressure (PIP): is the maximum airway pressure at the end of
inspiration.
⮚ The amount of air moved in and out of the lungs every minute is termed minute
volume (VT x respiratory rate).
⮚ Part of the inspired VT occupies conducting airways (anatomic dead space) which
does not contribute to gas exchange. Still another part of VT enters alveoli that are not
sufficiently perfused (alveolar dead space). Total dead space is the sum of anatomic
dead space and alveolar dead space.
⮚ Compliance is the dispensability of the lung and chest wall; that is, the change in
volume (ΔV) produced by a change in pressure (ΔP), or ΔV/ΔP. It is decreased with
surfactant deficiency, excess lung water, and lung fibrosis. It is also decreased when
the lungs are hyper-expanded.
⮚ Resistance is the impediment to airflow due to friction between gas and airways
(airway resistance) and between tissues of the lungs and chest wall (viscous tissue
resistance); that is, the change in pressure divided by the change in flow.
⮚ Work of breathing is especially important in the smallest infants and those with
chronic lung disease whose high airway resistance, decreased lung compliance,
compliant chest wall, and weak musculature may overwhelm their metabolic energy
requirements and impede growth.
3.3 Basics of ventilator breath and control of breathing during
mechanical ventilation
Goals: to understand how the ventilator provides breath to the baby; compare ventilator
breath with spontaneous breath and common ventilator modes to control and assist in
breathing.
In NICU mechanical ventilation of a patient requires the following components:
• High pressure gas source, (usually separate)
• Oxygen blender,
• Ventilator (controller of the flow), and
• Humidification system.
Basic design of a ventilator
• Ventilators have pressure reducing valves internally to modulate the operating
pressure of the ventilator
• The ventilator functions mainly as a controller.
• The output from the ventilator is a mechanical breath whose size and timing are
controlled and determined by pressure and flow waveforms.
• To achieve this, all ventilators have
• a control system (pneumatic, electrical or electronic) to regulate the pressure,
volume, or flow waveform, a cycling mechanism, and a system to provide end-
expiratory pressure
• All ventilators are equipped with mechanisms to provide four basic functions ( 4
phases of breathing):
1. initiate lung inflation, triggering
2. inflate the lungs with a tidal volume, inspiration
3. terminate lung inflation, cycling and
4. allow the lungs to empty, exhalation.
These 4 phases produce a ventilator breath.

Triggering, start of a breath, during mechanical ventilation
o Inspiration during ventilator breath can be triggered by a signal from the machine or
from the baby.
o When inspiratory flow starts with a ventilator-generated signal and is independent of a
patient-initiated signal, it is called ventilator-triggered breath
o When inspiration starts on a patient-generated signal and is independent of a
ventilator-generated signal, we describe it as patient triggered breath.
o In summary: a ventilator breath can be initiated by a trigger generated by the
o What are the variables or triggers that can be used to trigger a ventilator breath?
o The trigger to initiate a breath may be pressure, volume, flow, or time.
o The minimal pressure or flow that needs to be detected in the circuit can be set for any
patient-initiated breaths.
o When the patient is capable of making a strong effort, a higher threshold may be
chosen.
o However, when a patient’s inspiratory effort is weak or poor, the threshold should be
the lowest that the patient can trigger.
Cycling: switching from inspiration to expiration
During ventilator setting it is adjusted by setting the inspiratory time.
o Ventilator-cycling refers to ending inspiration based on signals from the ventilator
independent of signals based on patient factor ( Time-cycled)
o Patient cycling occurs when a signal based on the patient’s respiratory mechanics
reaches a threshold value.
Similar to the trigger, the variable to cycle a breath from inspiration to exhalation may be
pressure, volume, flow, or time.
What are the types of breath usually seen during ventilation and how to differentiate them?
When a baby on mechanical ventilation 2 types of breath can be recognized:
1. Spontaneous breath during which the start and end of a breath is determined by the
patient. So it can be described as patient-triggered and patient-cycled. There are 2
types of spontaneous breath that can be recognized: a) un assisted spontaneous
breath: when patient determines both the timing and size of the breath, b) assisted
breath: where the ventilator does some of the inspiratory work indicated by an
increase in airway pressure above the baseline. The patient must initiate a breath, and
then the ventilator is triggered to provide a positive pressure breath.
2. Ventilator breath, called mandatory breath: is the one in which the end of inspiration
is determined by the ventilator, independent of the patient. A mandatory breath may
be a) patient-triggered or b) machine-triggered. The inspiratory time is NOT under the
control of the patient
Spontaneous VS mechanical breath:
Spontaneous breath:

2. Can be un assisted or assisted
3. The pressure wave is negative
Spontaneous breath vs ventilator breath
Mandatory breath
1. The ventilator always controls the cycling ( end of inspiration)
2. Can be patient triggered or ventilator triggered
3. The pressure wave is positive.
3.4 Introduction To Conventional Mechanical Ventilation
Ventilator variables and control:
There are 4 main variables that need to be controlled by the ventilator to generate and control
the mandatory breath. These are the pressure (PIP), the volume (TV), the flow and the time
(Ti).
However only one variable ( e.g. pressure or volume) can be controlled ( and limited to a
peak ) during the inspiratory phase which becomes the independent variable and the other
variables vary according to the respiratory system compliance and resistance. The waveform
of the controlled variable will be fixed breath to breath
1. Pressure Control, PC :
• Pressure-control refers to the pressure waveform being controlled during inspiration,
usually a “square-wave” or rectangular waveform as well as the predetermined
pressure limit.
• During PC volume and flow vary in different cycles
• PRESSURE CONTROL IS THE COMMONLY USED MODE IN NEONATES
2. Volume Control, VC:
• With volume control, the shape of the volume waveform as well as the predetermined
volume limit is controlled.
• During VC pressure and flow are not fixed and vary in different cycles
• VOLUME CONTROL IS THE COMMONLY USED MODE IN PICU
3. Flow Control
• With flow control, the flow waveform is controlled while volume and pressure vary.
• When constant-flow inspiration is combined with time-cycling, it is identical to
volume-control and these terms may be used interchangeably.
• This type of ventilation is commonly used in pediatric patients ( not in neonates )
4. Time Control
• Time-control is a category of ventilator modes in which the flow, volume and
pressure during the set Ti depend on the mechanics of the respiratory system.
• High frequency oscillatory ventilation (HFOV) is an example.

Modes of Mechanical Ventilation:
Mode of ventilation is a predetermined pattern of interaction between the patient and the
ventilator. It includes the sequence of breaths, breath patterns, control variables within and
between breaths, and the schemes used to provide feedback as well as effecting the variables
during mechanical ventilation.
In the most recent recommendations published by the Paediatric Mechanical Ventilation
Consensus Conference, no specific mode of ventilation could be recommended over another.
Ventilator modes should be guided and chosen by clinician experience, patient
pathophysiology, institutional protocol, and ventilator availability. Each mode of ventilation
may be controlled via either pressure, volume or dual-control (DC).
Mechanical ventilators and their modes can be distinguished by the phase variables—trigger,
limit, and cycle—that govern the characteristics of the inspiratory phase of each breath:
⮚ The trigger regulates the start of each breath,
⮚ the limit sustains inspiration while
⮚ the cycling controls the termination of inspiration.
commonly used ventilatory modes in NICU
There are several modes used in conventional ventilation. However, in neonates the most
commonly used are
1. Assist Control mode (AC)
2. Synchronized Intermittent Mandatory Ventilation mode (SIMV)
3. Pressure support mode (PS)
4. Dual modes or Targeted modes
Assist Control Mode (AC)
• While using AC mode a patient can receive either a ventilator-initiated or patient-
initiated mandatory breath.
• Machine-triggered breaths are not preceded by a spontaneous breath.
• Patient-triggered breaths are preceded by a spontaneous breath which creates a
negative deflection in the pressure–time curve.
• Every patient breath is triggered by pressure or flow generated by the patient
inspiratory effort and “assisted” with either preselected inspiratory pressure (if PC) or
volume ( if VC ).
• When the patient does not make any effort of breathing such as with neuromuscular
blockade, the total number of breaths is equal to the pre-set ventilator rate
• Although useful in some patients, the AC mode cannot be used in the weaning
process, which involves gradual decrease in ventilator support.
• Ac mode can be used under pressure control (commonly for neonates) or volume
control (for PICU patients)
• This mode may be preferred in patients with little or no spontaneous respiratory effort
or those who require complete respiratory support .

Synchronized Intermittent Mandatory Ventilation (SIMV) mode
• SIMV is synchronized to the patient's inspiratory efforts. It is a rate mode
• A timing “window” appears just before the next mandatory breath is to be delivered.
If the patient initiates a breath in the timing window, then the ventilator will deliver a
mandatory breath synchronized to the spontaneous breath. If no spontaneous effort
occurs, then the ventilator will deliver a mandatory breath at the end of the timing
window.
• It is the preferable mode of ventilator therapy in infants who are breathing
spontaneously while on IMV.
• Since this mode allows patient to initiate some spontaneous breaths, the work of
breath may increase as the patient is breathing against ETT resistance. This can be
overcome by adding pressure support (PS see below) during inspiration to all
spontaneous breath. This is called SIMV with PS and it is preferred for SIMV alone.
• SIMV is a rate weaning mode
Pressure Support Ventilation (PSV)
• PS is a continuous spontaneous ventilation (CVS).
• All the breaths are spontaneous.
• Patient will trigger and cycle the breath,
• Ti (rate), PIP or VT are determined by patient for each breath
• All the breaths are supported with a preset positive pressure. (assisted spontaneous
breath)
• PS is a weaning mode and is not used for paralyzed or sick patients.

Dual-control modes of ventilation (Targeting schemes)
• Dual mode is a way of controlling two variables (pressure and volume), one variable
is directly controlled and the second one is controlled indirectly (guarantees or
targeted) through a feedback control used to deliver a particular pattern of breathing.
• The dual modes are sometimes described as targeting schemes. This is because while
the ventilator control one variable e.g. pressure, it will target or guarantee preset limit
for the other variable e.g. volume
• Examples of targeting schemes, dual modes
• Pressure regulated volume control, PRVC (with Maquet Servo series),
• Volume Grantee, VG, (Drager)
• Adaptive Pressure Ventilation (APV) (with Hamilton Galileo),
• Autoflow (Evita 4), or
• Variable Pressure Control (Venturi)
Why do we need to control tidal volume?
• There is increasing evidence to support that lung overstretching and overdistension
that causes lung injury rather than simply high pressures;And that volume trauma is
more serious than barotrauma ( lung trauma caused by high pressure).
Why volume control is not commonly used for ventilating neonates?
• Newborn infants are ventilated using un-cuffed endotracheal tubes. This may lead to a
variable leak around the endotracheal tube, and tidal volume cannot be controlled.
2. Volume-targeted ventilators.
Advances in technology for measuring delivered VTs have made these ventilators first-line
therapy for newborns with respiratory failure. Only volume-targeted ventilators specifically
designed for newborns should be used. Volume-targeted ventilators are always patient-
triggered.
General characteristics. Volume-targeted ventilators are similar to pressure-limited
ventilators except that the operator selects the targeted tidal volume ( TTV) delivered rather
than the PIP.
Volume guarantee
Is a mode of pressure limited ventilation, in which the ventilator targets an operator-chosen
VT (usually 4 to 6 mL/kg) during mechanically delivered breaths. Volume guarantee allows
rapid response of the ventilator pressures to changing lung compliance and may be
particularly useful in infants with RDS who receive surfactant therapy.
Pressure-regulated volume control (PRVC)
• is a modified pressure-targeted ventilatory mode, in which inspiratory pressure is
sequentially adjusted to deliver a target inspiratory volume with the lowest possible
pressures.
• Volume-targeted ventilators are particularly useful if lung compliance is rapidly
changing, as in infants receiving surfactant therapy.
• The pressure automatically varies with respiratory system compliance to deliver the
selected VT, therefore minimizing variability in minute ventilation and avoiding wide
swings in VT frequently seen with pressure-limited ventilators.
• Recent data suggest that volume-targeted ventilation reduces the risk of death or BPD
in extremely low birth weight infants, presumably by reduction of the risk of volu-
trauma (protective strategy).
• The system can be complicated and requires more skill to operate. Because VTs in
infants are small, some of the VTs selected are lost in the ventilator circuit or from air
leaks around uncuffed endotracheal tubes. Some ventilators compensate for these
losses by targeting expired rather than inspired VTs or by accounting for dead space
in the circuit.
3.5 High Frequency Ventilation Introduction
High frequency oscillatory ventilation (HFOV) utilises rapid ventilation rates with small tidal
volumes (often less than anatomical dead space) and active inspiratory AND expiratory
phases. A constant distending airway pressure is applied to the alveoli
which aims to maximise functional residual capacity and ventilation/perfusion matching, over
which small tidal volumes are superimposed at a high rate.
(HFV) is an important adjunct to conventional mechanical ventilation in newborns.
The aim of using HFOV is to reduce ventilator associated lung injury when high airway
pressures and volumes in conventional ventilation modes are required to maintain adequate
gas exchange ( secondary or rescue mode).
When initiated early ( primary mode), high frequency oscillatory ventilation may improve
oxygenation and reduce risk of lung injury in neonates and infants.
Indications For HFV
1. Alternative to CMV ( as primary mode)
2. When adequate oxygenation and/or ventilation cannot be achieved on CMV. ( as
rescue mode)
3. To minimise lung injury by avoiding use of high inspiratory pressures or FiO on
CMV.( primary or rescue )
Particular disease settings where HFOV may be appropriate include lung disease in:
o Neonatal Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS)
o Chronic lung disease of prematurity
o Meconium Aspiration Syndrome (MAS)
o Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia (CDH)
o Neonatal Air-leak Syndrome with pulmonary interstitial emphysema
o Pneumonia
o Pulmonary Haemorrhage
o Hypoplastic lungs
Types of High Frequency Ventilation
• Three types of high-frequency Three types of high frequency ventilators are approved
for use in newborns:
A. high frequency oscillator (HFO),
B. a high-frequency flow interrupter (HFFI),
C. and a high-frequency jet (HFJ) ventilator.
• High-frequency ventilation (HFV) refers to diverse modes of ventilation characterized in
general by supra-physiologic ventilatory frequencies (>60/min) and low tidal volumes.
• Commonly used high frequency modes are high frequency oscillatory ventilation
(HFOV) and high frequency jet ventilation (HFJV).
Ventilatory Control Parameters in HFOV
⮚ The main controls in HFOV are
1. mean airway pressure, MAP
2. oscillatory pressure, delta P, amplitude/power, bias flow,
3. frequency, F, and
4. inspiratory time, Ti.
Starting HFOV
Pre-Checks:
Ensure blood pressure and intravascular volume is adequate before transferring to HFOV, as
blood pressure may fall rapidly, especially in babies with perfusion problems in Sepsis /
NEC.
Consider invasive BP monitoring if possible.
Correct metabolic acidosis.
ETT leak - Consider upsizing ET tube
Initial settings of HFOV:
Mean Airway Pressure (MAP): Generally, the starting MAP is set 2-3cm abovethe current
CMV mean airway pressure. However, to achieve optimal lung recruitment the operator
should be prepared to start a recruitment manoeuvre.
Amplitude (ΔP):
Set the amplitude (delta P) to approximately double the value
of the MAP, sufficient to see a chest “wiggle” from the level of the nipple to the umbilicus.
Frequency/Hertz:
Usually frequency is set at 10 Hz. Lower frequencies may be used in severe lung disease,
with poor CO 2 clearance, especially in term infants.
E Ratio:
I:E ratio is usually 1:1 and not changed except in special circumstancesE Ratio: I:E ratio is
usually 1:1 and not changed except in special circumstances (e.g. severe gas trapping).
FiO2
Set appropriate FiO2 oxygen saturation range. and titrate according to patient response and
desired oxygen saturation range.
Immediate. Monitoring
Once stared on HFOV:
Obtain a blood gas within 20-30 minutes and adjust settings as appropriate.
Obtain a chest x-ray aftercommencing HFOV to determine lung expansion, ideally within
one hour. X-ray should show around 8 rib spaces.
The CXR should confirm the diaphragm to be lying between the 8th and 9th posterior ribs for
optimal lung inflation.Overinflation is indicated by:
• Diaphragm at 10+ ribs
• Intercostal bulging of the lungs
• Flattened diaphragm
• Thin cardiac silhouette
• Underinflation is indicated by:
• Lung fields with areas of collapse / consolidation
• Lung fields expanded to less than the 6th rib posteriorly
• High diaphragm
In specific situations such as non-uniform lung disease with one side of the lungs collapsed,
you might have to tolerate slight over distension in the good lung to encourage recruitment in
the other side.
Monitoring oxygenation and ventilation
It is very useful and practical to consider monitoring and adjustment of HFV on the basis of
oxygenation and ventilation.
Oxygenation
Main oxygenation control parameters are FiO2 and MAP.
FiO2:
Titrate according to patient response and desired oxygen saturation range.
MAP:
To improve oxygenation MAP can be increased gradually by 1-2 cm H2O. However high
MAPs ( > 12- 16) should be adjusted carefully as it may compomise the venous return and
lower arterial BP and worsen oxegenation . Whenever oxygenation is maintained, MAP
should be titrated and weaned gradually and carefully.
As discussed above adjustion of MAP is monitored by assessement of lung inflation on chest
x-ray.
Recruitment Manoeuvre
Is a stepwise increase in MAP of 1-2cmH O whilst monitoring response (oxygenation, CO 2
2 clearance, BP). Usually the MAP would be incremented every 5-10 minutes, but more rapid
increments in MAP, every 1-2 minutes, might be required depending on the clinical
condition, (for example, in a baby with severe oxygenation problem with a collapsed lung
volume).
Beyond the point of over-inflation (critical opening pressure) oxygenation will no longer
improve (and may deteriorate). MAP should then be reduced back to 2- 4cmH O below this
critical opening pressure.
Typical operating range for MAP will be between 10 to 16 If Higher MAPs are required,
Ventilation (CO2 clearance)
Ventilation (CO 2 clearance) in HFOV is controlled by 1) the ΔP (amplitude), for a given
level of lung inflation. It is also influenced by 2) the frequency of oscillation (Hz).
Decreasing the frequency can cause markedly increased CO2 elimination and should not be
done without discussion with the attending expert senior.
In response to pCO 2 measurements adjust the DP (amplitude) in increments of 2-4.:
a) Increase ΔP (amplitude) in response to a raised pCO2
b) Reduce ΔP (amplitude) in response to a low pCO2
Typical operating ranges for ΔP will be between 20 to 30cm H2O. Higher ΔP should only be
used with caution only in severe lung disease.
Always observe the chest wall to make sure that it is still vibrating. Recheck a blood gas 20
minutes after making a change.
Making Adjustments Once Established on HFOV:
Trouble Shooting During HFOV:
Low PO2: Consider:
1. ET tube patency and position – Check for chest movement/wiggle & breath
sounds, consider suction, while giving manual breaths with self inflation bag to check if ETT
is in the airway.
2. Condensation/ rain-out in the ventilator circuit- slight elevation of the oscillation to
assist with rain-out and enable good drainage.
3. Air leak/ Pneumothorax- Transilluminate, Urgent CXR, drain if needed
4. Sub-optimal lung recruitment- Increment MAP or recruitment manoeuver, consider
CXR
5. Over inflated lung –Check BP, reduce MAP; does oxygenation improve, Consider C-
XR
High PCO2: Consider:
1. ET tube patency and position : (as above)
2. Under-inflated lungs, insufficient alveolar ventilation :– Increase ΔP (amplitude) and
look for improvement in chest wall movement, could decrease frequency(Hz) after
discussion with expert senior.
The disadvantage of high MAP is “Over inflation of lungs” which leads to decreased cardiac
output and reduced BP, high pulmonary vascular resistance, decreased venous return and
pulmonary leaks. It can lead to poor oxygenation and tissue perfusion, eventually leading to
high CO levels in blood. It should be timely identified by means of clinical assessment, BP
and CXR and corrected by reducing the MAP.
Weaning
Weaning is primarily through reduction in the MAP as compliance improves, however it may
also be necessary to adjust ΔP +/- frequency (Hz), as CO2 clearance improves, to avoid
hypocarbia.
1. It is important to maintain the lung volume during weaning. Reduce FiO2 as tolerated, and
once less than around 30% begin weaning the MAP in increments of 1-2 cm H2O (except
when over-inflation is evident).
2.In air leak syndromes, reducing MAP may take priority over weaning the FiO2
3.Reduce ΔP (amplitude) in increments of 2-4, according to the paCO2. Remember to
observe the chest wall to confirm vibration.
4.If an acceptable paCO 2 cannot be maintained by adjusting the ΔP (amplitude) alone then
adjustments to the frequency (Hz) may be required. Changes in frequency should be
discussed with the expert senior.
5. Deterioration in oxygenation may be due to either a MAP which is too low (atelectasis), or
too high (over distension during the baby’s recovery phase). A C-XR may help to distinguish
these.
6. Patients may be extubated from HFOV e.g. to Vapotherm or CPAP. Alternatively, patients
may be transitioned to conventional ventilation prior to extubation.
When changing to conventional ventilation set an appropriate PEEP and then choose a PIP to
give a MAP 1 - 2 cm H2O below the HFOV setting.
7. Remember to wean sedation and start caffeine citrate, if indicated, in advance of
Potential Complications – HFO
1. Decreased cardiac output
2. Over-distension leading to pulmonary air-leaks
3. IVH due to changes in cerebral circulation related to treatment with the oscillaton.

3.6 VENTILATORY STRATEGIES AND SETTINGS
When strategizing mechanical ventilation for an individual patient, certain physiologic
parameters need to be assessed:
• Pathophysiologic considerations (disease process) e.g. RDS vs MAS. Post surfactant
therapy. Lung hypoplasia
• clinical findings
• blood gas analyses, (oxygenation vs ventilation)
• imaging studies.
Define your goal:
• to improve V/Q mismatch, (but to avoid O2 toxicity), or
• to recruit the lung, (but avoid lung trauma), or
• to support respiration, (plan for extubation as soon as indicated)
Initiation of Conventional Ventilation Pressure control mode in general:
• May start with
• PEEP: 4–6 cm H2O usually 5
• PIP: 14–25 cm H2O usually 16 to 20
• Rate: 30–60/min
• I:E ratio at least 1:2
3.7 Initiation of Conventional Ventilation According to Disease:
Respiratory distress syndrome (RDS):
Pathophysiology: RDS is caused by surfactant deficiency, which results in a severe decrease
in compliance (stiff lung) increasing the risk of pneumothorax. This causes diffuse alveolar
collapse with increased work of breathing.
Ventilator strategy: Is indicated when increased FiO2 and CPAP are inadequate to maintain
gas exchange, or in infants who tire from the increased work of breathing. The preferred
approach is to maintain the appropriate MAP with a TI initially set at 0.3 second and rate of
approximately 20 to 40 breaths per minute. Rarely, a longer TI is required to provide
adequate oxygenation. PIP is initially estimated by visible chest excursion and is usually 20
to 25 cm H2O.PEEP is usually set at 4 to 6 cm H2O. Higher PEEP may interfere with
cardiac output. Flow rates of 7 to 12 L/minute are needed to provide a relatively square
pressure waveform. Higher flows may be required at very high PIP (>35 cm H2O).
Apnoea:
Pathophysiology: Occasionally, apnoea is severe enough to warrant ventilator support,
even in the absence of pulmonary disease. This may result from apnoea of prematurity, or
during or following general anaesthesia.
Ventilator strategy: For infants completely dependent on the ventilator, the goal should be
to provide “physiologic” ventilation. moderate PEEP (3 to 4 cm H2O), low gas flow, and
normal rates (30 to 40 breaths per minute), PIP or VT adjusted to prevent hyperventilation
(10 to 18 cm H2O). Prolonged TI is unnecessary. For infants requiring a ventilator because of
intermittent but prolonged apnoea, low rates (12 to 15 breaths per minute) may be sufficient
Bronchopulmonary Dysplasia (BPD):
Pathophysiology:
⮚ Is an acquired chronic lung disease that occurs because of premature birth.
⮚ It results from injury to the alveoli and airways.
⮚ Bleb formation may lead to poor recoil.
⮚ Fibrosis and excess lung water may cause stiffer compliance.
⮚ Airways may be narrowed and fibrotic or hyper-reactive.
⮚ The upper airways may be over-distended and conduct airflow poorly.
⮚ BPD is marked by shifting focal atelectasis, hyperinflation, chronic and acute
increases in airway resistance, and a significant increase in the work of breathing.
Ventilator strategy:
⮚ Targeting oxygen saturations between 92 and 95%,
⮚ Use of large tidal volume to account for dead space, VT (8 to 12 ml/kg)
⮚ Adequate PEEP to avoid atelectasis and prevent airway collapse, (7 to 8 cm H2O)
⮚ Low set rate, (< 20 breaths/minute) with longer inspiratory times
⮚ Higher PIP are sometimes required (20 to 30 cm H2O) because of the stiff lungs.
Meconium aspiration syndrome (MAS):
Pathophysiology:
• MAS results from aspiration of meconium-stained amniotic fluid. The aspirated
meconium causes acute airway obstruction, markedly increased airway resistance,
scattered atelectasis, and hyper-expansion due to obstructive ball-valve effects.
• The indications for intubation include : worsening clinical distress, increased oxygen
requirements, worsening hypoxemia/acidosis, clinical instability and intolerance of CPAP
Ventilator strategy: Because of the ball-valve effects, the application of positive pressure
may result in pneumothorax or other air leak, so initiating mechanical ventilation requires
careful consideration of the risks and benefits.
• low ventilator rate (30/min), adequate expiratory time to minimize air-trapping with
inspiratory time 0.3–0.4 s.
• minimal PEEP that is needed to achieve sufficient oxygenation, 5 cm H2O
• PIP limited to 25 cm H2O
• If oxygenation is limited despite increasing PEEP to 7 cm H2O and/or PIP to more than
25 cm H2O to achieve a higher MAP, the infant likely needs more respiratory support and
high frequency ventilation should be considered.
• HFV has been successfully used in infants with MAS who are failing conventional
ventilation or who have air leak, slower frequencies (8 to 10 Hz) may be useful to
improve oxygenation and ventilation in severe cases.
Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia:
Pathophysiology:
⮚ It is a malformation resulting in the migration of intra-abdominal organs into the
thoracic cavity during fetal development.
⮚ This compromises fetal lung development, leading to pulmonary hypoplasia with
involvement of both ipsilateral and contralateral lungs.
⮚ Impaired branching morphogenesis, acinar hypoplasia, decreased terminal
bronchioles and failed alveolarization all contribute to decreased compliance and
FRC.
⮚ Gas exchange is impaired leading to severe hypoxemia.
⮚ Time constant is reduced due to reduced compliance.
Ventilator strategy:
⮚ Permissive hypercapnia (PaCO2 46–60 torr) is frequently practiced along with lower
target pre-ductal SaO2 (85–95%) and pH 7.25–7.40.
⮚ Lower peak inspiratory pressures PIP (< 25 cm H2O) are best to avoid
pneumothorax.
⮚ Mean airway pressures (MAP) can range from 12 to 18 cm H2O
⮚ HFOV can be used for hypercapnia or hypoxia/hypoxemia either as an initial or
rescue therapy after conventional mechanical ventilation did not improve clinical
status.

3.8 CARE & MONITORING OF A VENTILATED BABY
Monitoring & routine care:
• It is possible to monitor a variety of respiratory functions at the bedside in infants and
children.
• These include an assessment of gas exchange, lung mechanics, work of breathing,
neuromuscular capacity and the metabolic status of the patient.
• This chapter will briefly review some of the monitoring that is readily available at the
bedside.
• The parameters listed below should be assessed frequently to guide changes in the
ventilator settings.
• Care should be taken when any change is made.
• because adjusting one parameter is likely to affect the others.
Fraction of Inspired Oxygen.
• Inspired oxygen may be harmful to the lung parenchyma after prolonged exposure
due to the production of toxic oxygen-derived radicals.
• Although the precise threshold for concern is not known, it is desirable to reduce the
FIO2 to 0.5 (50% oxygen) or below as soon as possible, ideally within the first 24
hours.
• The primary determinants of oxygenation during mechanical ventilation are FIO2 and
mean airway pressure (Paw).
Humidification:
• Inspired oxygen may be harmful to the lung parenchyma after prolonged exposure
due to the production of toxic oxygen-derived radicals.
• Although the precise threshold for concern is not known, it is desirable to reduce the
FIO2 to 0.5 (50% oxygen) or below as soon as possible, ideally within the first 24
hours.
• The primary determinants of oxygenation during mechanical ventilation are FIO2 and
mean airway pressure (Paw).
Inspiratory Pressure (PIP)
• It reflects the pressure required to overcome elastic recoil and is the best estimate of
peak alveolar pressure, which is an important indicator of alveolar distension.
• Accurate measurement of Ppeak requires the absence of any patient effort during
inspiration or exhalation.
• Potential adverse effects from high inspiratory pressure include barotrauma,
volutrauma, and reduced cardiac output.
• Inspiratory plateau pressure should ideally be <30 cm H2O.
• Elevated Pplat may be reduced by decreasing PEEP, which may also decrease
oxygenation, or by decreasing VT, which may lead to a reduction in minute
ventilation.
• Permissive hypercapnia and a controlled reduction in pH may be accepted when high
Pplat must be reduced.
Relationship of Inspiratory Time to Expiratory Time and Auto-PEEP
• The total respiratory cycle time is calculated by dividing 60 seconds by the respiratory
rate.
• The times for inhalation (inspiratory time) and exhalation (expiratory time) occur
within the total cycle time and are termed the I:E ratio
• During spontaneous breathing, the normal I:E ratio is ~1:2,
• indicating that for normal patients, the exhalation time is about twice as long as
inhalation time.
• In chronic lung disease and other conditions associated with obstruction to expiratory
flow, such as asthma, the
• exhalation time becomes prolonged, and the I:E ratio changes (e.g., 1:2.5 or 1:3).
• The inspiratory time during volume breaths (AC or SIMV modes) is often determined
by the VT and inspiratory gas flow rate (flow × inspiratory time = VT).
Reduction in auto-PEEP can be accomplished by:
• Shortening the inspiratory time. This extends the expiratory time to allow full exhalation
of the VT ; however, it may cause alveoli with longer time constants to fill
incompletely.
• Decreasing the respiratory rate. This is the most effective way to decrease auto-PEEP.
• Decreasing VT. Increasing the inspiratory flow rate (volume breaths) is typically less
effective unless flow rates are set inappropriately low. The influence of a decreased
respiratory rate and VT on the PaCO2, pH, and minute ventilation must be considered.
Minute Ventilation:
• The primary determinant of CO2 exchange during mechanical ventilation is alveolar
minute ventilation (VA), calculated as:
VA = (VT- VD) × f
• where VD is dead space and f is respiratory rate.
• Physiologic VD represents, in general, lung units that are relatively well ventilated but
under perfused.
• The physiologic effect of increased VD is hypercapnia.
Monitoring patients on mechanical ventilator support: Require continuous monitoring to
assess the effects of treatment.
• Obtain a chest radiograph after intubation and intermittently as needed to evaluate
placement of the endotracheal tube and deterioration in status.
• Obtain arterial blood gas measurements after initiation of mechanical ventilation and
intermittently based upon patient status.
• Measure vital signs intermittently; frequently observe the patient directly (including
evaluation of patient-ventilator interaction).
• Measure inspiratory plateau pressure as clinically appropriate.
• Use continuous pulse oximetry to measure oxygenation.
• Use ventilator alarms to monitor key physiologic and ventilator parameters.
3.9 WEANING AND EXTUBATION OF A VENTILATED BABY
WEANING FROM MECHANICAL VENTILATION:
⮚ This process should be considered as soon as pulmonary function begins to improve.
Decisions concerning weaning are separate and apart from decisions concerning
extubation.
⮚ During weaning from mechanical ventilation, a patient gradually takes on more of the
function of gas exchange while the ventilator contributes less to the patient’s minute
ventilation.
⮚ The circumstances that required mechanical ventilation support must be resolved. In
addition, the patient must actively participate in the process, and objective and subjective
criteria must be set to monitor the success or failure of the process.
⮚ Factors that influence weaning from mechanical ventilation include:
● the patient’s level of alertness,
● need for sedative medication,
● respiratory drive and adequacy of oxygenation (SPO2 >95% with fractional excretion
of oxygen< 40% and or low PEEP requirements <7cmH2o),
● Adequacy of ventilation (PaCo2 <45 mmHg with no chronic respiratory failure, or
>45 mmHg with acceptable PH),
● the time elapsed since the patient’s most recent episode of respiratory or
hemodynamic decompensation.
⮚ Although previously thought of as a failed weaning attempt, it is currently endorsed by the
American College of Chest Physicians and the American Thoracic Society (ATS) to
extubate patients to preventive non-invasive ventilation. Multiple studies correlated
extubation to NIV with shorter intensive care length of stay and short-term mortality.
Predictors for successful extubation:
⮚ Once the neonate has achieved ventilatory settings when extubation seems to be a
reasonable next step, physicians should evaluate whether the patient is ‘ready’ or not for
extubation. This is a very important phase of this whole process since some patients can
be easily weaned to low settings but are not yet prepared to cope with respiration without
invasive support.
⮚ The following section will review the role of clinical factors, spontaneous breathing trials
(SBT) and autonomic nervous system function evaluation in assessing extubation
readiness in extremely preterm infants.

depends on the right balance between sympathetic and parasympathetic tones.
✔ The role of heart rate variability(HRV) and respiratory variability(RV) in predicting
disease in newborn infants is not as well understood.
✔ It has however gained popularity over the past years, especially with the latest
evidence that loss of HRV precedes the clinical presentation of late-onset neonatal
sepsis.

observational study of 56 preterm infants (birth weight ≤1,250 g) showed that HRV
was significantly decreased in those who failed extubation.

t: 3.10 COMPLICATIONS OF MECHANICAL VENTILATION
⮚ Mechanical ventilation (MV) is life-saving for many babies who require respiratory
support in the newborn period.
⮚ Paediatric patients and newborns in particular are anatomically and physiologically
than the increase in airway diameter which is a precipitating factor in why infants are
especially prone to hyperinflation and air trapping.
⮚ Unfortunately, infants who require mechanical ventilation frequently develop
complications. The most common ones are:
A. Lung injury and oxygen toxicity:
1. BPD is related to increased airway pressure and changes in lung volume, although
oxygen toxicity, anatomic and physiologic immaturity, and individual susceptibility also
contribute.
2. Air leak is directly related to increased airway pressure. Risk is increased at MAPs in
excess of 14 cm H2O.
B. Mechanical:
1. Obstruction of endotracheal tubes may result in hypoxemia and respiratory acidosis.
2. Equipment malfunction, particularly disconnection, is not uncommon and requires
functioning alarm systems and vigilance.
C. Complications of invasive monitoring:
1. Peripheral arterial occlusion with infarction
2. Aortic thrombosis from umbilical arterial catheters, occasionally leading to renal
impairment and hypertension
3. Emboli from flushed catheters, particularly to the lower extremities, the splanchnic bed,
or even the brain
D. Anatomic:
1. Subglottic stenosis from prolonged intubation; risk increases with multiple reintubations
2. Acquired tracheobronchomalacia from prolonged mechanical intubation
3. Palatal grooves from prolonged orotracheal intubation
4. Vocal cord damage
E. Ventilator associated pneumonia caused by nosocomial infection in the NICU. It can be
prevented by early extubation to minimize the time spent on the ventilator, changing
ventilator circuits only as needed, mouth care, and medical staff hand hygiene.
3.11 Mechanical Ventilation Trouble shooting:
▪ Sudden desaturation with high CO2: Disconnect the patient and bag;
⮚ If he improves, then check the ventilator (O2 source, increase Fio2, consider
mechanical or electrical failure).
⮚ Also check the tube for displacement, obstruction or Leak.
⮚ If he does not improve, now assess the baby for pneumothorax, hypoglycaemia,
hypotension, intraventricular haemorrhage and sepsis.
▪ Gradual desaturation with high CO2: This suggests inappropriate ventilator settings;
⮚ Increase PIP/ PEEP/ I:E ratio
⮚ Repeat blood gas.
▪ Gradual increase in PCO2 without gross changes in PO2: May be due to:
⮚ Insufficient tidal volume, rate or both
⮚ Increased dead space (long ETT, non-ventilated alveoli)
Actions:
⮚ Increase PIP by (2-5cm water), and/ or
⮚ Decrease PEEP by 1, and/ or
⮚ Increase rate by (5-10 bpm), and/ or
⮚ Shorten ETT if long to decrease the dead space.
▪ Decrease in PCO2 caused by over-ventilation:
⮚ Decrease the rate,
⮚ Decrease PIP and or increase PEEP.
